review.scope_assessment: This is a bounded re-adjudication of the single disputed MEDIUM finding GUEST-AUTHZ-LOCK-ORDER from the prior full-scope PR11 review, at the unchanged head 947cb691c. No source delta exists between the prior full review and this snapshot; only the disputed claim and the implementer's counter-trace/counterproof were assessed. Tracing GuestContexts.change() (packages/core/src/guest/context.ts:16) shows: (1) authorizeBookingActor(c,actor,['BOOKING_CREATE']) runs before `SELECT 1 FROM guest_contexts WHERE id=$1 FOR UPDATE`; (2) immediately after that FOR UPDATE lock is granted, `this.read(actor,c)` is invoked on the SAME connection/transaction c, and read() (context.ts:15) itself opens with `await authorizeBookingActor(c,actor,['BOOKING_VIEW'])` — a second, independent freshness check against the live guest_contexts row (revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at>inventory_clock()), executed as a fresh statement under default PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, which by definition observes the latest committed data as of that statement, i.e. post-lock-wait state. Both BOOKING_CREATE and BOOKING_VIEW are guest-permitted operations in the same `guestOperations` allow-list (booking-actor.ts:7) and both branch through the identical guest SQL predicate in authorizeBookingActor (booking-actor.ts:12-13); the operations list only affects the static allow-list check, not the revoked_at/expires_at freshness predicate, so there is no meaningful VIEW-vs-CREATE gap for this guest context. The original finding's own quoted evidence block contains the `const d=await this.read(actor,c);` line but its impact/condition text asserts change() "never re-validates authorization/revocation status after the lock is granted" without accounting for what read() does on that same connection — this is the specific point the finding missed. The provided real-PostgreSQL probe (two independent connections, one holding an uncommitted revoke/FOR UPDATE on the shared guest_contexts row while GuestContexts.change() runs on the actual guest role, with an explicit wait-on-pg_stat_activity assertion proving B genuinely blocks on the row lock before any resolution) reproduces exactly the sequence specified in the original finding's own "test" field, for both a mid-transaction revoke and an exact-24h-boundary expiry, and in both cases change() rejects with GUEST_CONTEXT_EXPIRED after the lock is granted, with the mutation callback never running and zero new holds/bookings. The probe's file-identity assertion against `git show <head>` confirms it ran against the unchanged reviewed code, not a patched variant. Taken together, static trace and the independent PostgreSQL evidence agree: the alleged authorization-freshness gap does not exist in the current code, because read()'s embedded authorizeBookingActor call supplies the exact post-lock recheck the original finding said was missing. This adjudication does not extend to any other file, revisit the declared launch/production gaps, or grant system-wide, production-readiness, or merge authorization; it resolves only the single disputed finding and its associated activation prerequisite from the prior review.

prior_finding_dispositions.evidence: The prior claim that GuestContexts.change() 'never re-validates authorization/revocation status after the lock is granted' is disproved by current code: change() calls this.read(actor,c) on the same connection/transaction immediately after `SELECT 1 FROM guest_contexts WHERE id=$1 FOR UPDATE` succeeds, and read() opens with authorizeBookingActor(c,actor,['BOOKING_VIEW']), re-running the identical revoked_at/expires_at freshness predicate as a fresh statement under default PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, which observes the row's just-committed post-lock state. This is not a product change (product_code_changed=false) but a correction of the original static trace, which overlooked the effect of its own quoted `const d=await this.read(actor,c);` line. Independent real-PostgreSQL evidence (probe source + verified stdout, file-identity-checked against `git show 947cb691c`) executes precisely the original finding's proposed reproduction for both a revoke-during-wait case and an exact-24h-expiry-during-wait case: in both, the calling side passes initial authorization, is observed genuinely waiting on the real FOR UPDATE lock, and after the blocking transaction commits/the clock advances, change() rejects with GUEST_CONTEXT_EXPIRED before the mutation callback runs, leaving the draft revision, hold count, and booking count unchanged. No counterexample to this recheck was found; the disputed defect does not exist in the unchanged code.
